answers_by_date.answer: Yes, but only for certain visa types and migrant statuses (e.g., economic, family, humanitarian, temporary or regular migrants)
answers_by_date.basis: Ley 18.469 (1985) was in force. Art. 2 barred public establishments from denying care or demanding prior payment. Arts. 5-6 gave full FONASA coverage only to affiliates (contributing workers, pensioners), their dependants and accredited indigents, and art. 6(d) covered pregnant women and children under six whatever their affiliation. Undocumented migrants could not be accredited as beneficiaries, so equal coverage reached only regular, documented migrants. I found no practice evidence for this period.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, but only for certain visa types and migrant statuses (e.g., economic, family, humanitarian, temporary or regular migrants)
answers_by_date.basis: Same statute; Ley 19.966 (GES) added art. 6(g) with effect from 1 July 2005. DS 110/2004 set the criteria for accrediting indigents but had no migrant-specific route (text not read). MINSAL dates its first special measures, for pregnant migrant women, to 2003; these were administrative only. I found no practice evidence contemporary with 2005.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, but only for certain visa types and migrant statuses (e.g., economic, family, humanitarian, temporary or regular migrants)
answers_by_date.basis: Ley 18.469 was consolidated into DFL 1/2005, Libro II (published 24 Apr 2006) with the same content. Administrative instruments (Resolución Exenta 1914/2008; Ord. A14 N°3229/2008) extended care to irregular migrant children under 18 and to pregnant women; they are not law and leave irregular adults uncovered. Liberona & Mansilla (2017) cite press-documented refusals of care around 2006-2008.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, but only for certain visa types and migrant statuses (e.g., economic, family, humanitarian, temporary or regular migrants)
answers_by_date.basis: Ley 20.584 art. 2 (published 24 Apr 2012) added a general right to timely care without arbitrary discrimination for every person, but no FONASA entitlement for undocumented adults. DS 67 was signed 29 May 2015 but published only on 10 Mar 2016, so it does not count on this date. Practice: INDH 2013 and the Arica/Iquique cases of 2013-2014 cited by Liberona & Mansilla show barriers for undocumented migrants.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but they are not the same

answers.sourcing_note: The Ley 18.469 text and its 2004-2006 amendments, and DS 67 with its publication date, were read on LeyChile. I did not read the texts of DS 110/2004 and Constitution art. 19 Nº 9 (pages truncated), nor the 2003/2008 administrative instruments (known only from MINSAL and academic descriptions). Practice evidence for 2000 and 2005 is essentially absent.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The protection answer holds for 2020, but it rests on DS 67 (in force 10 Mar 2016) read with Ley 18.469/DFL 1 and Ley 20.584, not on Ley 21.325 art. 15, which was not yet in force. The implementation rating 'Usually; Effectively Always' looks high: MINSAL itself acknowledges persisting barriers and discrimination against undocumented migrants, and Liberona & Mansilla (2017) document breaches of the rules.
answers.notes: Relied on statutes and decrees only; no court ruling was used. The 2003 pregnant-women measures, Res. Exenta 1914/2008 (children under 18) and Ord. A14 3229/2008 are administrative instruments, not law, so they do not by themselves change the protection answer before 2016; they are treated as practice.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, but only for certain visa types and migrant statuses (e.g., economic, family, humanitarian, temporary or regular migrants)
answers_by_date.basis: DS 44/1988 (Sistema General Unificado de Subsidio Habitacional) and DS 62/1984 governed housing subsidies. DS 44 art. 4 opened the subsidy to adult natural persons enrolled in the DS 62 Registro, with no nationality clause; I read the 2002 wording, not the 2000 wording. Enrolment required an identity document and a socio-economic file (inferred), so only documented, regular migrants could apply. Emol (2016) says subsidies to foreigners were 'almost anecdotal' as late as 2006; I found nothing closer to 2000.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, but only for certain visa types and migrant statuses (e.g., economic, family, humanitarian, temporary or regular migrants)
answers_by_date.basis: DS 40/2004 (in force 19 Mar 2004) replaced DS 44; DS 62/1984 stayed in force. I found no explicit rule on foreigners. DS 174 (Fondo Solidario de Vivienda) was published only on 9 Feb 2006. Practice: Emol reports 482 subsidies to foreigners in 2006.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, but only for certain visa types and migrant statuses (e.g., economic, family, humanitarian, temporary or regular migrants)
answers_by_date.basis: Decreto 184 (Diario Oficial 31 Mar 2009) amended DS 174 art. 4: foreign applicants must hold a Certificado de Permanencia Definitiva, so only permanent residents qualify. The 2006 and 2008 versions of art. 4 had no such clause. Practice: Emol reports subsidies to foreigners rising from 482 in 2006.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, but only for certain visa types and migrant statuses (e.g., economic, family, humanitarian, temporary or regular migrants)
answers_by_date.basis: DS 49/2011 (published 26 Apr 2012), DS 1/2011 (published 6 Jun 2011) and DS 174 all required permanent residence; DS 105/2014, which rewrote DS 49 art. 3(b), was published only on 20 Mar 2015. Emol reports that MINVU dropped a five-year seniority requirement on the permanent-residence document in October 2014, and that 1,673 foreign families received subsidies in 2015.

practice_sources.title: Emol, Subsidios habitacionales para extranjeros se han cuadruplicado en la última década

answers.sourcing_note: I read the DS 174 versions of 2006, 2008 and the current text with its amendment notes, the current DS 44 text with its amendment notes, the DS 105 text and the 2020 DS 49 text on LeyChile. The DS 62/1984 registry rules, the 2000 wording of DS 44 art. 4, and the foreigner clauses of DS 40/2004, DS 1/2011 and the original DS 49 could not be read (pages truncated). The 2014 seniority change is known only from press. Practice evidence is one press data piece and says nothing on irregular migrants.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The protection answer holds, but its 2020 basis is the MINVU subsidy decrees (DS 49 art. 3(b), DS 174 art. 4, DS 1/2011), which require permanent residence; Ley 21.325 art. 18 was not in force in 2020. 'Effectively Always' for implementation is not backed by any cited evidence.
answers.notes: No court ruling was used. The 2000-2005 answers rest on DS 44's silence on nationality together with an inferred documentation requirement. The dated narrowing is Decreto 184 (31 Mar 2009), which limited DS 174 to permanent residents. The band stays 'certain statuses' throughout, but the covered group changed: possibly any documented resident before 2009, permanent residents after.
